doc.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Chicago's harmonic pianists and Bill Lee's teaching
summary: He credits Bill Lee and Chris Anderson for teaching him harmony, and describes Chicago pianists, Ahmad Jamal, Nelson Riddle's orchestrations, and Chicago singers and his Benny Carter date.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Chris Anderson. He said Herbie Hancock studied with him. A harmonic genius. And he came up with Bill Lee who was another genius, who was Spike Lee’s father, that’s the way I could put it, no people know about Bill Lee too much but he’s Spike Lee’s father. Harmonic genius. He was the one that taught me how to play music. Because when I heard him play in Chicago he was playing these chords and I said wow man, what kind of stuff is that? Now you had got away from Phineas playing, you know the two hands and swinging and orchestrating which is good, but when I heard these I call them harmonic gestures, I said man I’ve never heard no stuff like that. But see in Chicago, all piano players had their own harmonic devices. That’s why, you know, and believe it or not it’s still the most underrated city when it comes to musicians in jazz, if you can believe it, yeah. They’re underrated. Well the people say what about the Memphis musicians? I say well we don’t even count. They say wait a minute, what are you talking about. I say we were nonexistent. And it’s the truth. But the musicians, but all the piano players in Chicago had certain harmonic devices. When I used to go to Richard Muhal Abrams’ house, he had a certain way. He would play a straight ahead like Bud Powell. You know what I’m saying. But everybody had a harmonic concept. Floyd Morris, Ronnell Bright who was Nancy Wilson’s accompanist. All the piano players that played. There was a legendary pianist there named Sonny Thompson who was like rhythm & blues, he could sit down and play like Art Tatum. You see what I’m saying? So that’s how I learned, so when I Bill Lee playing all these beautiful harmonics I said man, I’ve got to find out what © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

that is. You know. So it took me two weeks before he would open up to me and he showed me, he talked to me about what he was doing, then he told me about Chris Anderson and Billy Wallace and naturally Mr. Ahmad Jamal was holding court at the Persian Lounge another harmonic genius, a true musical genius. I mean everybody knows how I feel about Ahmad and Phineas, that those are my two favorite piano players bar none, and they don’t have a problem with it, you see what I’m saying. But back to about the singers, that’s how you play for singers. You have to listen and let them sing and you become the orchestra. And see we used to listen to Nelson Riddle, Frank Sinatra in “The Wee Small Hours of the Morning.” And when you listen to it you hear that it was a match made in heaven, the way Frank would sing and Nelson would, through his orchestration, he’d do strings and the violin and muted trumpets with the flute and the French horn, oh man. Nothing greater. And then when Herbie and I used to get together there was a great arranger and orchestrator, it was probably the greatest orchestrator that ever lived, his name was Robert Farnon. And he did some dates with J.J., he did a date with Joe Williams, “Here’s to Life,” and Herbie had records by him called the “Cross Five [inaudible] and Herbie and I used to listen to all those kind of things, and me being dumb I made a mistake and said, “Oh by the way, Herbie, I stealed your two Robert Farnon records.” “Yeah man, give me my records.” I should have kept my mouth shut. So but like I said Chicago was a harmonic town. You had singers like Lorez Alexander or Lurlean Hunter one of the greatest singers that Carmen McRae was in awe of. I think she’s related to Clark Terry. Teri Thornton who played piano and sang, she got the I think the National Endowment one year and a couple of years later she was gone. So Chicago was a great city for that. Because you had to know how to play for singers, you have to know how to transpose, you had to play in all the keys, you had to play ballads. I played with Gene Ammons and you had to know how to play real slow. I played with Benny Carter — I did a gig with him called “Inside Benny Carter,” one of the greatest records he’s ever made. They didn’t put the personnel on it but there’s Roy McCurdy, Bob Cranshaw and yours truly. We rehearsed twelve hours a day for that date. It’s called “Inside Benny Carter.” I think they put it out on CD. So that’s always been my thing you know. And when I got to New York, and like I say Hank Jones was scoping me out and I didn’t even know it. And I played with all the singers at Birdland. Now don’t ask me how it happened, I don’t know. Maybe I played with one and word got around, and I’d be working opposite Coltrane. I played with Johnny Hartman way before McCoy and Trane. Johnny Hartman wouldn’t leave home without me. I played with Arthur Prysock and I had to take off and I had Herbie Hancock to play Saturday night and Cedar Walter was there to confirm it. I had all the singers.
